title: Quiz: What Is a Statistical Model?

questions.text: In the equation y = f(x) + ε, what does ε represent?
options: The fitted value predicted by the model
Random variation that no model can explain
The slope of the regression line
The difference between two model families
questions.explanation: ε (epsilon) is the noise — irreducible random variation due to measurement error, unobserved factors, and pure chance. f(x) is the signal (fitted value).

questions.text: What is the difference between a model family and a fitted model?
options: A model family is for training data; a fitted model is for test data
A model family defines the equation shape; a fitted model is the specific member closest to the data
A model family always has more parameters than a fitted model
There is no difference — the terms are interchangeable
questions.explanation: The model family (e.g., all straight lines y = a1 + a2·x) defines the shape. The fitted model is the one specific line whose parameters were estimated from the observed data.

questions.text: In the statistical modelling cycle, you only need to fit a model once and then you are done.
questions.explanation: Modelling is iterative. After fitting, you inspect residuals; if they show patterns, you revise the model family and refit. The cycle repeats until residuals look like random noise.

questions.text: What does it mean when a residuals-vs-predictor plot shows a clear curved pattern?
options: The model fits the data perfectly
The noise ε is normally distributed
The model has captured all the systematic variation
There is remaining structure the model has not captured — the model family is likely misspecified
questions.explanation: A curved pattern in residuals means the model missed a non-linear component. The residuals should look like random scatter if the model family is correctly specified.

questions.text: George Box's quote 'All models are wrong, but some are useful' implies that:
options: We should never use statistical models because they are always wrong
A model does not need to be literally true to be practically useful for describing data
Useful models always have zero residuals
The best model is the one with the most parameters
questions.explanation: Box's point is that a model is an approximation — it simplifies reality. The relevant question is not 'Is it true?' but 'Is it useful/adequate for describing the data and making predictions?'
